name: Pärnu
title: Pärnu Coaster and Cargo Ship Thickness Gauging | Gulf of Riga
description: Thickness measurement in Pärnu for timber, peat and general cargo coasters: hull, hold, hatch cover and ballast tank gauging in the Gulf of Riga's river port.
h1: Ultrasonic Thickness Measurement for Coasters at the Port of Pärnu
intro: Pärnu, best known as Estonia's summer resort, also has a working river port at the mouth of the Pärnu River, in the north-east corner of the Gulf of Riga. Small and medium coasters load sawn timber, wood products and peat here and handle some general and bulk cargo, and many are older ships on short-sea charters. Owners use Pärnu calls for condition gauging, renewal-survey preparation and pre-purchase checks. Technicians fly from India to the ship for each job, as nobody from Atlantis is based in Estonia.

highlights.p: Pärnu's trade is wood and peat: sawn timber, chips and horticultural peat loaded onto coasters bound for the Baltic and North Sea. Loading takes time, which leaves room to gauge holds, hatch covers and ballast tanks alongside.

highlights.h: A river berth with shallow approaches
highlights.p: Ships reach Pärnu across Pärnu Bay and through a dredged channel into the river mouth, which limits their size. The fleet calling here is small short-sea tonnage, where thin plating needs careful calibration and a dense reading pattern.

The shallow bay freezes in most winters, and icebreaking may be needed to keep the port open. Ships that trade here in the cold months take ice wear on their bows and waterlines, and owners follow up with spring checks.

port.h: Pärnu's river port and the coastal trade
p: Pärnu sits at the head of Pärnu Bay, an inlet at the north-eastern corner of the Gulf of Riga, where the Pärnu River enters the sea. The town is Estonia's best-known seaside resort, with beaches, spas and a yacht harbour, but the cargo port on the river has the longer history, going back to Pärnu's days as a Hanseatic trading town. Ships come in from the Gulf of Riga across the shallow bay, follow a dredged channel into the river mouth and berth at quays along the river banks. The limits of that channel make Pärnu a port for small and medium coasters rather than large bulk carriers, and draught is the first thing a charterer checks when fixing a ship here.

Cargo is dominated by the forests and bogs of south-west Estonia. Sawn and planed timber, wood chips and pellets, and peat for horticulture are loaded for buyers around the Baltic and the North Sea, and some general and bulk cargo comes in for local industry and construction. The ships are short-sea general cargo coasters, many with box-shaped holds suited to timber and peat, often carrying a deck cargo of timber on top. Many are older ships under a range of European flags, owned by small companies that manage one vessel or a handful, which shapes the gauging they ask for: practical condition checks, renewal-survey preparation and steel planning sized to a small ship.

The year at Pärnu has two halves. In summer the bay is calm, the resort is busy and cargo moves steadily, with coasters loading over a day or two. In winter the shallow bay freezes early, the Estonian Transport Administration sets ice restrictions for the port, and icebreaker assistance keeps the channel open in a hard winter; coasters without a suitable ice class may stay away until spring. Water levels in the Gulf of Riga change with the wind far more than with the tide, and strong south-westerly gales can push the level in Pärnu Bay up sharply while easterlies draw it down, which matters for draught at the river berths. A gauging plan at Pärnu has to respect both the season and the depth.

facilities.h: Where coasters are gauged at Pärnu
p: All of our Pärnu work is planned alongside at the river quays. Timber and peat coasters are measured hold by hold before loading begins or during pauses, with hatch covers, coamings and deck plating done while the cargo is being brought to the quay. Ballast tanks and the double bottom are entered once the crew has ventilated them and issued an entry permit. On these small ships the plating is thin and corrosion gathers in the lower holds, the ballast tanks and around the hatch coamings, so the reading pattern is dense and every reading is tied to a frame number on the sketch.

We do not plan dockings at Pärnu, so the coasters that trade here go elsewhere when they need one: Tallinn Shipyard on Estonia's north coast, or repair yards in Klaipėda, Gdańsk and other Baltic ports that take small cargo ships. A Pärnu call is useful as the step before: the owner can have the ship measured, receive a steel estimate and ask yards to plan the work on real figures rather than guesses. Anchorage work in the shallow bay is not something we plan.

context.h: Inspection, ice and the coaster trade from Pärnu
p: Pärnu is an Estonian port, so port state control is carried out by the Estonian Transport Administration as part of the Paris MoU. General cargo coasters are not among the regime's highest-risk ship types, but age and a poor inspection record raise a ship's risk profile, and many of the coasters calling here are old enough for that to count. Deficiencies on ships of this kind often involve hatch covers, corroded air pipes and vents, and structural wastage in holds and ballast tanks, which is exactly what a sensible gauging scope covers. Owners who know their ship's condition before an inspection are better placed to answer an inspector's questions.

The timber and peat trades bring their own wear. Timber deck cargoes put lashing loads into deck plating, coamings and lashing points, peat is acidic and its wet dust settles in hold corners, and repeated loading by grab or loader damages hold sides and tank tops. In winter, ice in Pärnu Bay and the Gulf of Riga wears the bow and waterline, and the ice restrictions for the port decide which coasters can keep trading through the cold months. Ships calling from outside the EU need an Inventory of Hazardous Materials on board under the EU Ship Recycling Regulation, a document that matters when an older coaster is sold or finally goes for recycling.

jobs.h: Typical gauging jobs for coasters at Pärnu
jobs.p: Pärnu jobs are mostly practical work for small owners. Renewal-survey preparation on older coasters, condition gauging when an owner wants to know how much life a ship has left, and pre-purchase gauging when a coaster changes hands are the most common requests. Hatch cover and coaming gauging often comes up after a timber or peat receiver complains about wet cargo, and post-winter checks of the bow and waterline follow a cold season on the Gulf of Riga. Scopes are kept in proportion to the ship's size and trade, and planned so they finish within the loading period.

logistics: The team flies into Tallinn Airport, or Riga Airport across the Latvian border, and drives to Pärnu, which lies on the main road between the two capitals. Estonia and Latvia are both Schengen states, so one Schengen visa covers our technicians from India on either route, and we apply as soon as the loading date is firm. The ship's agent arranges access to the river quays. Because coaster schedules shift with weather and cargo readiness, we stay in close contact with the agent in the days before boarding.

faqs.q: Is Pärnu deep enough for the ships you gauge?
faqs.a: Pärnu takes small and medium coasters, limited by the depth of the bay and the river channel, and those are the ships we gauge here. Their plating is thinner than on deep-sea ships, so we use probes and calibration suited to thin steel and a denser reading pattern. Larger ships trading in the Gulf of Riga are more likely to be gauged at Riga or another deeper port.

faqs.q: Can holds be gauged while timber or peat is being loaded?
faqs.a: Partly. Holds are measured before loading starts, the lower areas first because they are buried as soon as cargo goes in. Hatch covers, coamings and deck can be done while cargo is being brought to the quay, and ballast tanks once the crew has made them safe to enter. We agree the sequence with the master so the gauging never holds up loading.

faqs.q: Can you gauge coasters at Pärnu in winter?
faqs.a: Yes, when they are calling. Pärnu Bay freezes in most winters, and coasters without a suitable ice class may avoid the port until spring, but those that trade through the cold months can be gauged alongside as usual. Inside the ship, cold affects ventilation times and our choice of couplant; outside, ice against the hull limits shell readings.

faqs.q: Where do Pärnu coasters go for docking?
faqs.a: Owners usually send them to repair yards elsewhere on the Baltic, such as Tallinn Shipyard on the north coast of Estonia or yards in Klaipėda or Gdańsk. Gauging the ship at Pärnu first gives the owner and the yard a measured steel estimate, so the docking can be planned and booked for the right length of time.

faqs.q: What does a pre-purchase gauging cover on a coaster?
faqs.a: Typically the holds, ballast tanks and double bottom, deck and hatch covers, and selected shell plating reachable from inside, measured against the original thicknesses. The buyer gets a summary of where wastage is close to or beyond the allowable limits, with sketches and photographs, and an idea of the steel renewal ahead. We agree the extent with the buyer's adviser before the inspection.
